concepts.name: Constitutional Basis and Legislative Competence of EPA 1986
key_dimensions: Article 253 as the primary constitutional hook (Stockholm Conference 1972) vs. concurrent list Entry 17A/17B
How EPA 1986 overrides state laws under Article 253 read with Entry 13 of Union List
Directive Principles under Articles 48A and 51A(g) as supplementary justification
Distinction from Water Act 1974 and Air Act 1981 which derive power from Article 252 (state consent required)

concepts.name: Definition of 'Environment' and 'Environmental Pollutant' under EPA 1986
key_dimensions: Expansive definition of 'environment' under Section 2(a): water, air, land and their interrelationship with living organisms
Distinction between 'environmental pollutant' (Section 2(b)) and 'environmental pollution' (Section 2(c))
Inclusion of noise as an environmental pollutant — a frequent UPSC trap
Contrast with narrower definitions in Water Act 1974 and Air Act 1981

concepts.name: Powers of the Central Government under EPA 1986: Scope and Extent
key_dimensions: Section 3: Omnibus power to take all measures for protecting and improving environment quality
Power to issue directions under Section 5 — binding nature on all persons and authorities
Delegation of powers to officers/authorities under Section 23 and its limits
UPSC trap: EPA gives powers to Central Government only, NOT to state governments directly

concepts.name: Section 5 Directions: Nature, Scope and Judicial Interpretation
key_dimensions: Power to issue written directions to any person, officer, or authority including closure, prohibition, and regulation orders
Overriding effect: Section 5 directions override all other Acts except essential services
Judicial interpretation in Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India on enforceability
Comparison with Section 33A of Water Act and Section 31A of Air Act — overlap and supremacy

concepts.name: Environmental Quality Standards and Schedule Provisions
key_dimensions: Section 6: Rule-making power to prescribe standards for emission/discharge of pollutants
Distinction between 'standards for quality of environment' and 'standards for emission/discharge'
Schedules under EPA Rules 1986: Schedule I (standards), Schedule II (procedures for taking samples), Schedule VI (general standards)
UPSC trap: Standards under EPA are minimum national standards; states cannot set more lenient standards but CAN set stricter ones

concepts.name: EPA Rules 1986: Key Provisions and Procedural Requirements
key_dimensions: Rule 3: Standards for emission/discharge of environmental pollutants
Rule 13: Prohibition and restriction on handling hazardous substances
Procedure for taking samples (Rules 4-6) and admissibility as evidence
Mandatory prior notice requirement before taking samples — a procedural trap in questions

concepts.name: Prohibition and Restriction on Location of Industries: Section 3(2)(v) and EIA Linkage
key_dimensions: Section 3(2)(v): Power to restrict areas where industries may/may not be established
Linkage with Environment Impact Assessment (EIA) Notification 2006 as a subordinate instrument
Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) Notification as an exercise of EPA powers
UPSC trap: EIA Notification has no independent statutory basis — it derives entirely from EPA 1986

concepts.name: Persons Authorized to Perform Functions: Section 4 and Delegation Framework
key_dimensions: Section 4: Central government may appoint officers with designated powers and functions
Difference between 'authorized persons' under Section 4 and 'authorities' constituted under Section 3(3)
Relationship between EPA-authorized officers and CPCB/SPCB officials
UPSC trap: CPCB and SPCBs are NOT created under EPA 1986; they are created under Water Act 1974

concepts.name: Offences, Penalties and Enforcement Mechanisms under EPA 1986
key_dimensions: Section 15: Penalty for contravention — imprisonment up to 5 years or fine up to ₹1 lakh or both, with enhanced punishment for continuing offence
Section 16: Offences by companies — liability of person-in-charge AND the company (vicarious liability)
Section 17: Offences by Government Departments — Head of Department liable; contrast with immunity under other Acts
UPSC trap: After 7 years of continuing offence, minimum imprisonment is prescribed — a specific numerical fact

concepts.name: Cognizance of Offences: Section 19 and Locus Standi
key_dimensions: Section 19: No court shall take cognizance without a complaint by the Central Government or its authorized officer
60-day notice requirement before a citizen can file a complaint — critical procedural requirement
Comparison with NGT Act 2010 where any 'aggrieved person' can approach directly
UPSC trap: Courts cannot take suo motu cognizance under EPA; NGT can take suo motu cognizance

concepts.name: Citizen Suit Provision and Public Participation Framework
key_dimensions: Section 19 proviso: Citizens can file complaints after giving 60-day notice to government — narrow locus standi
Contrast with broader PIL route under Articles 32 and 226 used to bypass Section 19 restrictions
Judicial expansion of citizen participation through PILs: MC Mehta cases
Comparison with US Citizen Suit provisions that inspired Indian framework

concepts.name: Hazardous Substances Regulation under EPA: Sections 6, 7, 8
key_dimensions: Section 7: Prohibition on discharge of environmental pollutants in excess of prescribed standards
Section 8: Handling of hazardous substances only in compliance with prescribed procedures
Manufacture, Storage and Import of Hazardous Chemicals Rules 1989 as subordinate legislation
UPSC trap: Hazardous Waste Management Rules are under EPA 1986, NOT under the Factories Act 1948

concepts.name: Duty to Furnish Information: Section 9 and Accident Reporting
key_dimensions: Section 9: Mandatory duty to report accidents causing/likely to cause pollution to authorities
Obligation on persons handling hazardous substances to provide information and render assistance
Linkage with Bhopal Gas Tragedy as the direct catalyst for this provision
Consequences of non-reporting vs. consequences of the polluting event itself — separate offences

concepts.name: Entry and Inspection Powers: Section 10 and Section 11
key_dimensions: Section 10: Power of authorized persons to enter/inspect premises, examine/test equipment, and seize records
Section 11: Power to analyze samples — only analysts appointed under Section 13 can give valid analysis
Distinction between 'analyst' appointed under EPA and analysts under Water/Air Acts
UPSC trap: Without authorization under Section 4 or Section 10, entry/inspection is NOT valid under EPA

concepts.name: Environmental Laboratories and Government Analysts: Sections 12 and 13
key_dimensions: Section 12: Central government can establish/recognize Environmental Laboratories
Section 13: Appointment of Government Analysts to analyze samples sent to labs
Evidentiary value of analyst reports in court proceedings under EPA
Distinction from NABL-accredited labs — only Section 12 labs are valid for EPA enforcement purposes

concepts.name: Notifications Under EPA: CRZ, EIA, Eco-Sensitive Zones as Statutory Instruments
key_dimensions: All major environmental notifications (CRZ 2019, EIA 2006, ESZ notifications) derive authority from Section 3(1) and 3(2) of EPA
Legal challenge to EIA 2006 Draft Amendment (2020) — importance of EPA as parent statute
Eco-Sensitive Zones (ESZ) around Protected Areas notified under EPA — not under Wildlife Protection Act
UPSC trap: Violation of CRZ/EIA conditions is prosecuted under EPA 1986, not under separate CRZ/EIA laws (they are notifications, not Acts)

concepts.name: Relationship Between EPA 1986 and Other Environmental Laws: Hierarchy and Overlaps
key_dimensions: EPA as 'umbrella legislation' — overarching framework vs. specific Acts (Water, Air, Forest, Wildlife)
Section 24: EPA overrides inconsistent provisions in other Acts (except Water and Air Acts where harmonious construction applied)
UPSC trap: EPA does NOT repeal Water Act 1974 or Air Act 1981 — all three co-exist with EPA having residuary jurisdiction
Role of NGT Act 2010 as the adjudicatory complement to EPA's regulatory framework

concepts.name: Precautionary Principle and Polluter Pays Principle: Judicial Embedding into EPA
key_dimensions: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996): SC read Precautionary Principle and Polluter Pays into EPA via customary international law
Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India: Absolute liability of polluters for remediation costs under EPA framework
Distinction between 'precautionary principle' (prevent harm) and 'polluter pays' (remedy harm) — separate doctrines often confused
How these principles supplement the text of EPA without explicit mention in the Act

concepts.name: Protection of Bona Fide Actions: Section 18 and Good Faith Immunity
key_dimensions: Section 18: No suit/prosecution against government or officers for actions taken in good faith under EPA
Limits of good faith protection: malicious/arbitrary actions not protected
Comparison with similar immunity provisions in Water Act (Section 63) and Air Act (Section 55)
UPSC trap: Good faith immunity under Section 18 does NOT extend to private companies or individuals

concepts.name: EPA 1986 and the National Green Tribunal: Jurisdictional Interface
key_dimensions: EPA 1986 is one of the seven scheduled Acts under NGT Act 2010 — NGT has jurisdiction over EPA violations
NGT can impose penalty, direct restoration, and award compensation for EPA violations
UPSC trap: NGT cannot handle matters relating to Wildlife Protection Act, Forest Act, or Indian Forest Act — those are NOT in NGT's schedule
Conflict between High Court PILs and NGT jurisdiction over EPA matters — Supreme Court's resolution in Madhya Pradesh HC v. NGT
